title: POC scoping - private networking & data residency - Mendwell Health
summary: Discovery / scoping call for a 6-week POC to validate private networking and data residency for Mendwell Health. Key goals: prove low-latency inference in us-east-1 with VPC peering or PrivateLink, meet security requirements (no internet egress for PHI, KMS integration, SOC2 evidence), and size dedicated capacity for ~60 concurrent sessions at peak. Team agreed to run a benchmark harness (50/200/800 token distribution) and exchange security docs + network diagram.
action_items: Samir to share private networking architecture doc and sample VPC peering config (due 2028-02-18)
Maya to provide benchmark harness repo and runbook for load tests (due 2028-02-17)
Ravi to provide network CIDR ranges and list of allowed egress endpoints (due 2028-02-16)
Jenna to confirm internal stakeholders and success criteria doc (due 2028-02-20)
Diego to schedule a follow-up bench test kickoff (propose times by 2028-02-19)
next_steps: Send Private Networking diagram + sample CloudFormation for PrivateLink and VPC peering
Exchange security questionnaire and SOC2 artefacts
Run baseline latency + throughput benchmark in Mendwell's VPC with Redwood Private agent (48 hour test window)
Agree on POC timeline: 2-week setup, 2-week benchmarks, 2-week integration/validation
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Lin (Redwood SE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE); Jenna Morales (Mendwell VP Eng), Dr. Alan Pierce (CTO), Ravi Kumar (Security Architect), Lena Cho (Platform Eng), Tommy Hsu (DevOps)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Discussed private networking approaches (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), data residency to us-east-1 and eu-west-1, egress constraints for PHI, and POC success criteria. Action items assigned for docs, CIDRs, and benchmark runbook.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time on Valentine's day, I know it's late in the week - I'm Samir from Redwood, AE for Mendwell. Quick intros?
[00:10] Jenna: Hi Samir, Jenna Morales, VP Engineering at Mendwell, joining with Alan and Ravi.
[00:15] Alan: Alan Pierce, CTO.
[00:18] Ravi: Ravi Kumar, Security Architect.
[00:20] Maya: Maya Lin, Solutions Engineer at Redwood. Diego's on as well.
[00:24] Diego: Hey everyone.
[00:27] Samir: Cool. Goal for today's call is to scope the POC around private networking and data residency - specifically your constraints around PHI, region requirements, and what success looks like. We'll also size the workload so Maya can propose the right Dedicated or Private configuration.
[00:40] Jenna: Yep that's right. High level - Mendwell wants to run a pilot feeding clinical summarization and triage flows. Data must not leave our VPC, no internet egress for PHI, and we need KMS integration for key management. Timeline wise we'd like to start as soon as possible, ideally next week for initial setup.
[00:56] Samir: Understood. Quick question on model footprint: are you planning to use our hosted Redwood API variants or run Redwood Private in your VPC?
[01:05] Jenna: We're leaning Private. Compliance team is firm on keeping data in our network. But open to discussing PrivateLink if that helps speed things up.
[01:15] Maya: For Private deployments we support a private control plane and a customer-managed data plane that stays in your VPC. Two common options: VPC peering / Transit Gateway or AWS PrivateLink. Both can work; tradeoffs are route tables and cross-account peering complexities.
[01:30] Tommy: Quick clarifying q - are we able to run everything in us-east-1? Our main data resides there.
[01:34] Samir: Yes, Redwood's private offering can be pinned to us-east-1. We also have eu-west-1 for EU residency if needed.
[01:40] Ravi: Important: no logs with PHI can be forwarded to external storage. We can allow telemetry that is metadata only, but audit logs must be inside our logging account.
[01:50] Diego: Noted. We typically allow customers to configure log-forwarding to an internal S3 or ELK cluster inside the VPC. We also support disabling transcript retention on the control plane for sensitive queues.
[02:03] Maya: On KMS, we support customer-managed keys (CMKs) integrated with AWS KMS or HSMs for on-prem. You can bring your own key and we won't hold the plaintext.
[02:14] Ravi: Good. Do you have documented attestation for SOC2 and encryption at rest?
[02:18] Samir: Yes, we'll share the security pack - SOC2 report redacted, encryption whitepaper, and the KMS integration guide after this call.
[02:26] Jenna: Great. Now on sizing - at peak we expect about 60 concurrent sessions hitting the summarization endpoint. Average session makeup is 1-3 requests, with a token distribution: 50% short prompts (~50 tokens), 40% medium (~200 tokens), 10% long (~800 tokens).
[02:45] Maya: That's really helpful. For an initial POC we usually recommend a small dedicated pool - maybe 2x A100-equivalent nodes to validate latency SLOs, then scale. Can I ask what latency SLO you're targeting?
[02:59] Alan: Ideally sub-200ms p50 for the 50-200 token requests, and sub-500ms p95. If that requires quantized models or batching tradeoffs we can discuss.
[03:12] Maya: Makes sense. For the token sizes you described, with our optimized runtime and low-latency kernels, 2 GPUs could hit ~150ms p50 for medium requests if we avoid heavy batch windows. We'll run a benchmark to validate.
[03:25] Samir: To be explicit on success criteria: 1) All PHI must stay in our VPC or be encrypted with CMK we control, 2) p50 latency <200ms for medium requests, p95 <500ms, 3) throughput of at least 50 req/s sustained during benchmark window, 4) integration with SAML SSO for console access and RBAC for operator personas. Anything to add, Jenna?
[03:48] Jenna: Also: network topology documented and approved by our infra team, and a clear rollback plan if we detect data leakage.
[03:55] Ravi: And demo of audit logs showing per-request traceability.
[03:58] Maya: We can provide tracing hooks and token-level cost/latency breakdowns in the Console. For traces we can stream to your X-Ray or Datadog - or keep them internal to your logging account.
[04:10] Tommy: Regarding PrivateLink vs VPC peering - what are the tradeoffs for cross-account routing and egress?
[04:16] Diego: PrivateLink is usually simpler for cross-account access, you expose an NLB endpoint in your account and we create the interface endpoint. No route table changes across accounts. VPC peering or Transit Gateway gives more flexibility if you want routing into multiple subnets but requires additional route config and sometimes approval from networking teams. PrivateLink also prevents transitive routing which can be good for security.
[04:38] Ravi: For us, PrivateLink sounds preferable since it reduces our blast radius. But we need to understand IP whitelisting and whether the connector makes any outbound calls to the public internet for model updates.
[04:50] Maya: Model updates are pulled via the control plane by default, but in Private deployments we can sync model artifacts via a customer bucket or via a managed pull over the private link. We'll document that.
[05:00] Jenna: About egress - we need to prevent any traffic to external endpoints except to our monitoring endpoints.
[05:05] Samir: We'll include config options to restrict egress; the standard pattern is to put the Redwood runtime in private subnets with NAT disabled for data plane, and only allow outbound to your own S3 or artifact buckets.
[05:18] Ravi: What about benchmarking - what's the plan and what do you need from us?
[05:22] Maya: We'll run a two-phase benchmark: baseline (Redwood-hosted simulation to validate config) and on-prem/VPC run. For the VPC run we need: CIDR ranges, endpoint subnets, security group rules, and sample payloads (anonymized or synthetic to avoid PHI). We'll provide a harness repo that runs token distribution tests (50/200/800) and measures p50/p95/p99 latency and token throughput.
[05:45] Jenna: We can provide synthetic payloads and the CIDRs. How long do you expect the VPC benchmark to take?
[05:50] Maya: The test harness can run for a 24-72 hour window to smooth out variability; for the POC we'd propose a 48-hour steady-state test.
[05:58] Diego: We also recommend enabling KV cache and prefix caching during the second half, to show cost savings and latency improvements. Note: "KV cache" is often pronounced as "K-V cash" in transcriptions - just a heads-up, you'll see that in the logs.
[06:10] Samir: (laughs) Noted.
[06:13] Alan: Any constraints around encryption in transit - do you support mTLS between your runtime and the control plane?
[06:17] Maya: Yes, we support TLS 1.3 and mTLS for control plane signals. Data plane traffic is entirely inside your VPC for Private - so you control the TLS termination if you want.
[06:27] Ravi: How do we verify no unexpected egress? Can we run a packet capture or flow logs during the benchmark?
[06:33] Diego: Absolutely, we encourage VPC Flow Logs and packet captures for the first tests. We'll work with your DevOps to create a checklist.
[06:40] Maya: Also, for the Console access, we can integrate SAML SSO and map groups to RBAC roles. We'll provide an SAML metadata XML and steps to set the attribute mappings.
[06:52] Jenna: That should be fine. Cost question: for Dedicated capacity vs Private, what's the expected monthly burn for the initial config?
[06:59] Samir: Ballpark for 2 A100-equivalent GPUs reserved, with a small control plane and network egress minimized, we'd estimate $Xk/month - I'll put precise numbers in the pricing doc. For the POC we can offer short-term reserved pricing or a time-boxed trial credit to make it easier.
[07:15] Ravi: Need to see a clear breakdown, including potential data transfer costs between accounts if PrivateLink is used.
[07:20] Samir: We'll include that.
[07:22] Jenna: Ok timeline recap?
[07:24] Samir: Proposed POC timeline: Week 0 (this week) - exchange docs, network CIDRs, kickoff. Week 1 - infra setup (PrivateLink / VPC peering), Week 2 - baseline internal tests & run benchmark harness (48 hours), Week 3-4 - integration & validation, finalize success criteria and handoff. Overall 4-6 weeks depending on approvals.
[07:43] Ravi: Sounds reasonable. We'll need security signoff in Week 1.
[07:46] Samir: Action items then: Samir to send networking archetype diagram + PrivateLink and peering CF templates; Maya to send benchmark harness + runbook; Ravi to share CIDRs and allowed egress list; Jenna to share success criteria doc and stakeholders. Diego to propose times for bench kickoff.
[07:59] Jenna: We'll aim to turn around CIDRs and stakeholders by Friday.
[08:03] Maya: One more question - are there any model quantization options that might affect fidelity for clinical summaries?
[08:09] Diego: Yes, we have quantization profiles. For clinical text we typically avoid heavy quantization on initial runs to preserve fidelity, then test int8 variants to evaluate cost/latency tradeoffs.
[08:21] Alan: We'll want to see a quality regression report if you test quantized models.
[08:25] Maya: We'll include that in the benchmark outputs.
[08:28] Samir: Great. Any other open questions?
[08:31] Ravi: One last: audit logs retention - default retention in your console is 90 days, but we need 7 years for some compliance. Can we push logs to our own S3 with lifecycle policies?
[08:43] Maya: Yes - that's supported. We'll show the configuration in the security pack.
[08:48] Jenna: Thanks everyone. I think we're aligned.
[08:50] Samir: Cool, we'll send the docs right after this call and propose times for the bench kickoff. Thanks all.
[08:56] (call ends)
